title: Prompt Cache: Modular Attention Reuse for Low-Latency Inference
one_line: Precomputes and stores the KV attention states of reusable prompt segments ("prompt modules") declared in an XML schema, then concatenates them at request time to skip most of the prefill and cut time-to-first-token.

repo.evidence: Paper section 1 (p.2) states 'Our source code and data used for evaluation are available at github.com/yale-sys/prompt-cache'; repo/README.md:3 links back to the paper and README.md:241-246 carries its BibTeX; the yale-sys org matches the authors' Yale CS affiliation. The repo contains the real system (promptcache/cache_engine.py implements 3.3/3.4, promptcache/schema.py implements the PML of 3.2, promptcache/model/{llama2,falcon,mpt}.py are the 4.2 position-ID-aware architectures), not a placeholder.
repo.badge_evidence: none found - MLSys 2024 ran a voluntary artifact-evaluation process (mlsys.org/Conferences/2024/CallForPapers) but no badge appears on this paper's proceedings entry or PDF

H1_open_repo.evidence: Official repo github.com/yale-sys/prompt-cache named in paper section 1 (p.2). 8,902 lines of Python; core system present: promptcache/cache_engine.py (523 lines, SchemaCache._process at 185-307 = module encoding, CacheEngine.process at 388-522 = cached inference), promptcache/schema.py (534 lines = PML modules/unions/parameters), vendored position-ID-aware models in promptcache/model/. Eval harnesses eval.py, eval_sys.py, eval_acc.py, get_scores.py present. Not binary-only, not plotting-only.

H2_no_root.evidence: Pure Python/PyTorch installed with pip (requirements.txt); no Dockerfile in repo_facts.json top_level; no kernel module, eBPF, /proc/sys, hugepage or KVM usage anywhere. Timing uses torch.cuda.Event (promptcache/generation_engine.py:104-114, eval_sys.py:338-351) and torch.profiler (eval_sys.py:413), which are CUPTI-based and unaffected by perf_event_paranoid=3. The only repo_facts red flag is 'multi_node' at g.sh:1, which is an srun wrapper with --nodes=1 --ntasks=1; every .slurm file requests --gpus-per-node=1 (eval_sys_a40-7b-gpu.slurm:14) and is an optional NCSA Delta convenience.

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: Headline config is Llama2-7B on ONE GPU (paper 5.1: 'LLMs that fit within the memory capacity of a single GPU (40 GB)'; eval_sys_a40-7b-gpu.slurm:14 requests 1 GPU), loaded 8-bit (config/llm_config_llama2_7b.json:5) with max_ctx_length 4096 (:8) - fits 24 GB on the A5000 (Ampere SM 8.6, same generation as the paper's A40). Prompt modules are stored in host DRAM (promptcache/cache_engine.py:290-292); at Table 2's 0.5 MB/token for a 7B model a 3.5K-token module is ~1.75 GB, trivial in 125 GB. Noted concerns, not fails: config/llm_config_falcon_40b.json and llm_config_mpt_30b.json (Table 1's 30B/40B rows) will not fit 24 GB and are out of scope; Figure 4's CPU numbers are reproducible in kind but not magnitude on a 16-core Zen 3 vs the paper's i9-13900K.

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: All deps pip-installable in user space (requirements.txt; torch 2.3.0 cu121 wheels run on driver 535 via minor-version compatibility, nothing is compiled). Undeclared but pip-installable: bitsandbytes + accelerate (needed by load_in_8bit=True at eval.py:36, eval_sys.py:37, eval_acc.py:79) and sentencepiece/protobuf for LlamaTokenizer (promptcache/model/__init__.py:188). The bleurt/TensorFlow submodule in README lines 15-20 is avoidable: it is imported only by benchmark/metrics.py:3, which no eval entry point uses (eval.py/eval_acc.py/get_scores.py import the top-level metrics.py). Data: THUDM/LongBench from HF, public and non-gated (benchmark/longbench.py:90); schemas are generated at runtime (benchmark/longbench.py:124-126). Weights: meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf is gated, but the repo itself configures ungated substitutes that the paper also evaluates in Table 1 - tiiuae/falcon-7b-instruct (config/llm_config_falcon_7b.json) and mosaicml/mpt-7b-chat-8k (config/llm_config_mpt_7b.json). No proprietary traces.

reproduce.target: Figure 3 (paper section 5.2.1), Llama2-7B on one Ampere GPU: TTFT of Prompt Cache with prompt modules in CPU memory vs the KV-Cache baseline across LongBench datasets, supporting the claim of a 1.5-3x TTFT reduction (yellow bars). Stretch within the same run: the 5-10x GPU-memory-resident bars (the abstract's 8x) after guarding the .cpu() demotion at promptcache/cache_engine.py:290.
reproduce.scale_down: One RTX A5000 24 GB instead of three GPUs; report a single Ampere point next to the paper's A40 and drop the A100/4090 columns. Llama2-7B-chat in 8-bit (the repo default), falling back to config/llm_config_falcon_7b.json if the HF licence gate blocks Llama. Keep max_tokens=3500 / max_ctx_length=4096 unchanged. Figure 4's CPU-inference arm optional on 2-3 datasets only.
reproduce.effort: 3-4 person-days + ~5 GPU-hours (env + gated-weight workaround + four script fixes + a plotting script). +1 person-day and ~6 CPU-hours for the CPU-inference arm. Reproducing Table 1 at full LongBench scale would be a further ~30-60 GPU-hours and is out of scope for the first two weeks.
reproduce.rationale: M, not H: four separate edits are required before the headline figure can be produced at all - eval_sys.py:432-437 has the two run_latency_eval() calls commented out and calls run_critical_point22() instead; the output directories benchmark/results_latency and benchmark/aaa are never created outside run_latency_eval (eval_sys.py:313); bitsandbytes/accelerate are undeclared; and the Llama weights are gated. The headline GPU-resident-module variant is not reachable by any flag (cache_engine.py:290-292 always demotes to host, and TokenSequenceCache.upload()/free() at :65-73 are dead code). There are no plotting scripts (benchmark/results/README.md is a one-line stub), get_scores.py:73 reads ./results_13b/ while eval.py:155 writes ./benchmark/results/, and the pins are two years old (transformers==4.34.0 forces a Python 3.10 env). M, not L: the harness, datasets, runtime schema generation, baseline arm and metric all exist and map directly onto Figure 3; the model fits the GPU at paper scale; nothing needs hardware we lack; and README.md:85-104 gives an annotated demo.py smoke test with expected TTFTs to anchor against. No artifact badge exists to raise confidence.

addons.name: Budgeted co-encoding (scaffold groups): memory-for-quality instead of compute-for-quality
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that precomputing co-encoded KV for a small selected set of prompt-module groups (the paper's unimplemented 'scaffolding') recovers most of the accuracy lost to genuinely independent modular encoding - measured as the LongBench F1/accuracy gap versus full prefill - at a bounded cache-memory overhead, on multi-module prompts (multi-document QA and passage retrieval) where Table 1 already shows Prompt Cache's largest regressions.
addons.mechanism: (i) Add a true independent-encoding mode: encode each module in its own forward pass instead of slicing it out of a whole-scaffold pass, so the section 3.3 approximation is the one actually measured - today SchemaCache._process runs ONE forward over the entire scaffold (cache_engine.py:221-248) and slices per-TokenSequence KV out of it (:261-296), so modules silently attend to their predecessors. (ii) Populate the empty cache_l2: encode chosen module groups (start with adjacent pairs) together and store the group KV as an override that CacheEngine.process prefers when all members are imported - exactly the semantics section 3.3 specifies. (iii) Add a memory-budgeted selection policy: rank candidate groups by mean L2 deviation between a module's independently-encoded and co-encoded V tensors (one extra forward per candidate) and greedily admit until budget B is spent. (iv) Sweep B in {0, 0.25x, 0.5x, 1x} of L1 cache size and plot accuracy vs memory vs TTFT, since larger groups also mean more bytes copied per request.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 3.3 names scaffolding as the remedy for semantically dependent modules and frames it explicitly as a memory/quality trade - and the artifact does not implement it: cache_l2 is typed (cache_engine.py:171), initialised (:179) and read (get_cache_l2, :316-322) but never written anywhere in the repo (verified by grep). Table 1's Passage Retrieval drops 7.50->4.25 (Llama2-7B) and 9.08->6.50 (13B) and 2WikiMQA drops 16.63->13.95, so the degradation regime is real and flagged by the paper's own bolding. Separately, the whole-scaffold encoding shortcut means Table 1 probably understates the damage of true modular reuse - establishing that is itself a result. Also benchmark/longbench.py:105 wraps the whole document in a single <module name="context">, so the accuracy evaluation barely exercises modularity at all.
addons.feasibility_rationale: All four pieces are localized: an alternate encoding loop in SchemaCache._process, a dictionary that already exists (cache_l2), a lookup added before get_cache_l1 in CacheEngine.process, and a schema-generator tweak in benchmark/longbench.py to emit multi-module schemas. Scaffold (schema.py:439-523) already knows how to materialise an arbitrary module selection. Well under 1-2k LOC, no new serving infrastructure, evaluated with the repo's existing accuracy harness (eval.py + get_scores.py) on one 7B model in 8-bit. Cost is capped by sampling ~100 entries on 3-4 LongBench datasets (~10-15 GPU-hours per arm), which fits this machine.
addons.research_value_rationale: It tests whether the paper's central accuracy claim survives the encoding discipline the paper says it uses, and it explores the complement of everything in the follow-up literature: spend MEMORY to restore cross-module attention rather than COMPUTE. Both outcomes teach something - if co-encoding proves unnecessary, the 'LLMs tolerate discontinuous position IDs' claim is strengthened at module granularity; if it proves necessary, Prompt Cache's memory model (Table 2) is materially understated and the reported speedups are optimistic. A reviewer at MLSys would care about either.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'CacheBlend cross-attention KV cache fusion reused text chunks recompute EuroSys 2025'; 'prompt cache modular attention reuse follow-up KV cache eviction policy non-prefix modules 2025'. Closest work attacks the same problem with RECOMPUTATION, not precomputed groups: CacheBlend (EuroSys'25 best paper, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3689031.3696098, arXiv 2405.16444) selectively recomputes the top-k tokens with the largest V-value discrepancy; EPIC, KVLink, A3 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.17560) and CacheClip (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.10129) do position-independent linking or trainable cross-chunk tokens. No work found that precomputes co-encoded module groups under an explicit memory budget, and none that audits Prompt Cache's own scaffold-slicing shortcut. Honest framing for the course paper: memory-for-quality vs compute-for-quality on one GPU, with CacheBlend as an implementable baseline rather than a scoop.

addons.name: Cost-aware tiered prompt-module cache (admission, eviction, prefetch)
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that a cost-aware GPU-residency policy that ranks prompt modules by (recompute_time - transfer_time) per byte, rather than by recency or frequency, reduces mean TTFT relative to LRU, LFU and Prompt Cache's current usage-counter staging, under a multi-schema workload with Zipfian module popularity and a GPU cache budget well below the working-set size.
addons.mechanism: Turn PromptCache into a real two-tier cache. (i) Actually use TokenSequenceCache.upload()/free() (currently dead code) so admitted modules stay resident in HBM across requests instead of being re-copied every request. (ii) Replace the current staging rule in PromptCache.update - sort by usage_counter, keep the longest matching prefix of the previous layout, re-copy the rest - with a pluggable policy interface, and implement LRU, LFU, a size-aware GDSF variant, and a cost-aware policy whose value comes from the measured per-length (recompute - upload) crossover that eval_sys.py's run_critical_point already produces. (iii) Add optional prefetch driven by <union> structure, which section 3.2.3 explicitly suggests. (iv) Build the missing workload generator: today the harness adds one schema, serves one prompt, then calls remove_all_schemas() (eval.py:280, eval_sys.py:363), so no cross-request reuse is ever exercised; the generator must hold N schemas resident and draw module sets from a Zipf distribution. Report hit rate, bytes copied, and the TTFT distribution.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 4.1 states verbatim: 'We leave the development of a system that incorporates cache replacement and prefetching strategies to future research', and section 6 repeats it. Section 5.5 notes that at 0.5-2.5 MB/token a working set of 'hundreds of prompt modules' is 'tens of gigabytes' - larger than a 24 GB GPU - so the policy question is forced on exactly this machine. The artifact's dead TokenSequenceCache.upload()/free() (cache_engine.py:65-73, never called anywhere) shows the tier was anticipated but never populated, and cache_engine.py:118 carries the authors' own TODO 'adopt in-place sorting to reduce redundant host-device memory copies'. Figure 5 already gives the crossover data (host->device 5.34 ms vs device->device 0.23 ms at 5K tokens) that a cost-aware policy needs.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The cache code is small and the policies are textbook, but this is cross-cutting: cache engine changes plus an entirely new multi-schema workload generator plus new metrics (hit rate, bytes copied, TTFT distribution), because every existing script measures a single request against a cold, immediately-destroyed cache. Compute is cheap - prefill-only, 7B 8-bit, one GPU - and cache budgets are enforced in-process so no cgroup or root tricks are needed. But it is a genuine 10-week, multi-student scope rather than a localized patch.
addons.research_value_rationale: A reviewer would recognise the question as the paper's own stated gap, and a prompt module is a genuinely different caching object from a prefix block: non-prefix, variable-size, position-pinned, with a known recompute cost. But tiered KV caching is a crowded area and 'cost-aware beats LRU' is close to an expected result; the surprise would have to come from the crossover regime, where short modules are cheaper to recompute than to ship across PCIe.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'hierarchical GPU host KV cache tiering eviction prefetch LLM serving AttentionStore CachedAttention ATC 2024'; 'prompt cache modular attention reuse follow-up KV cache eviction policy non-prefix modules 2025'. Closest: CachedAttention/AttentionStore, USENIX ATC'24 (https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc24-gao-bin-cost.pdf) - multi-tier HBM/DRAM/disk KV cache with scheduler-aware prefetch and eviction, but for multi-turn conversation PREFIXES; SGLang HiCache (https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2025-09-10-sglang-hicache/) - hierarchical radix-tree prefix cache across GPU/CPU/disk; and learned prefix-cache eviction ('Not All Tokens Are Worth Caching', arXiv 2605.18825). All are prefix-tree structured; none handles schema/module structure, position-ID pinning, or the recompute-vs-transfer crossover for arbitrary composable segments. Not scooped, but the novelty must be argued on module granularity and the prefix-caching policies should be cited and ideally emulated as baselines.

addons.name: Quantized module store plus a per-module compute-or-load rule
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that storing prompt modules in INT8 (and INT4) per-head-quantized form, combined with a per-module rule that recomputes modules shorter than the measured transfer/compute crossover instead of shipping them over PCIe, reduces TTFT for GPU inference with host-resident modules - the paper's weakest configuration at 1.5-3x (Figure 3, yellow bars) - without a measurable LongBench score change on a 24 GB Ampere GPU.
addons.mechanism: The artifact already exposes the right seams: store_k_hook/store_v_hook are applied when a module's KV is captured (cache_engine.py:284-285) and read_k_hook/read_v_hook when it is handed back to the model (cache_engine.py:513); all four are identity functions today (promptcache/model/__init__.py:116-126). Implement (a) per-head/per-channel affine INT8 and INT4 quantization in the store hooks with dequantization in the read hooks, so only quantized bytes cross PCIe; (b) a per-module dispatch in CacheEngine.process that consults a calibration table produced by the repo's own run_critical_point (eval_sys.py:88-215) and recomputes short modules on the GPU rather than uploading them; (c) measure the cache_time and prefill components separately (they are already separated at cache_engine.py:391-509) plus accuracy via eval.py + get_scores.py. FP8 is not an option on this machine (A5000 is SM 8.6), so INT8/INT4 via torch integer ops is the target.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 6 names both halves as future work: 'the integration of compression techniques in the KV cache, or utilization of grouped query attention'. Section 5.5 makes the memory case (2.5 MB/token at 70B 'leaves CPU memory as the only option'). Section 5.4 measures host->device at 5.34 ms vs host->host 3.79 ms and device->device 0.23 ms for 5K tokens - for GPU inference the PCIe copy IS the overhead, and it is exactly the difference between the 1.5-3x and 5-10x bars in Figure 3. The four unused hooks in promptcache/model/__init__.py are the authors marking where this belongs.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Quantization inside the existing hooks is a contained change of a few hundred LOC; the calibration harness (eval_sys.py run_critical_point) already exists; evaluation runs on the repo's own scripts with one 7B model in 8-bit on one GPU. The only real subtlety is matching the dtype/layout the vendored models expect where past_key_value is concatenated (promptcache/model/llama2.py:363-364).
addons.research_value_rationale: The direction is well trodden and the headline outcome (INT8 nearly free, INT4 costs some accuracy) would not surprise anyone. What is less expected, and worth the experiment, is the interaction: once modules are 2-4x smaller the compute-or-load crossover moves, and the optimal decision may flip for a whole class of module sizes. That interaction, measured on a single-node PCIe budget rather than a network link, is the defensible part - but this is the weakest of the four on novelty.

scoop_check.details: Query: 'KV cache quantization compression to reduce host-to-device PCIe transfer latency cached context loading CacheGen'. Closest: CacheGen, SIGCOMM'24 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3651890.3672274) compresses KV into bitstreams for NETWORK fetch, 3.5-4.3x over a quantization baseline; 'Compute or Load KV Cache? Why not both?' (Cake, https://arxiv.org/html/2410.03065v1) explicitly overlaps loading and recomputing; ZipCache/KIVI-style KV quantization is standard. Both ingredients exist separately. Not scooped for the modular, host-to-device, single-node setting, but the honest positioning is 'port two known techniques into Prompt Cache and measure the crossover shift', which still works as an improvement paper while being the least novel option here.

addons.name: Cross-request module sharing in a batch
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that materialising a shared prompt module's KV once per batch (as a broadcast view or block table) rather than once per request increases sustained throughput and the maximum feasible batch size for prompts drawn from a common schema on a 24 GB GPU - a benefit the paper argues arithmetically in sections 3.4 and 5.4 but never measures.
addons.mechanism: The serving path is strictly batch-size-1: CacheEngine.process returns a single token-id list and both eval.py:192-198 and generation_engine.py:96-102 add a redundant batch dimension with unsqueeze(0); PromptCache's device buffer is allocated as [num_head, max_ctx_length, head_dim] with no batch dimension (cache_engine.py:104-107). Add a batched path that (i) groups queued prompts by schema, (ii) builds a per-batch KV where shared modules are expand-ed (stride-0) rather than copied and unshared suffixes are padded, (iii) supplies the additive attention mask so padded slots are ignored - the vendored LlamaModel._prepare_decoder_attention_mask (promptcache/model/llama2.py:798-819) already composes a causal mask with a padding mask, so the hook exists - and (iv) measures tokens/s and peak torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated against batch size, versus a per-request-copy control.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 3.4 ('Memory optimization in batch inference') and section 5.4 both claim the benefit numerically - '100 requests, each with a 2K token prompt ... reduce the memory footprint by 50%' - with no experiment. Section 6 lists 'GPU primitives for sharing attention states across concurrent requests' as future work and notes it would improve TPOT, the one latency component Prompt Cache currently cannot touch (section 5.4 reports TPOT unchanged at ~32 ms/token). The repo has no throughput harness at all: every script measures a single request.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The most invasive of the four: it touches the cache engine, the generation loop, and the vendored attention/mask code, and it needs a new throughput harness that does not exist. It is squarely doable on one GPU with a 7B 8-bit model, but it is a full 10-week multi-student job and carries a real risk that the expand-ed view is materialised anyway by the torch.cat at promptcache/model/llama2.py:363-364, silently erasing the benefit - which the team would have to detect and engineer around. The frozen transformers-4.34 vendoring also rules out simply adopting a modern paged-attention kernel.
addons.research_value_rationale: vLLM and SGLang already share PREFIX blocks across requests by reference counting with copy-on-write, so the concept is established; the contribution is demonstrating it for non-prefix, schema-composed modules with discontinuous position IDs and quantifying the batch-size/throughput headroom the paper only asserted. Solid and measurable, but expected, and a reviewer would press on the marginal novelty over prefix sharing.

scoop_check.details: Query: 'sharing non-prefix KV cache blocks across concurrent requests in a batch paged attention modular reuse throughput 2025'. Paged-attention block sharing with reference counting and copy-on-write is standard practice; recent work refines shared-prefix paging and prefix-shared decoding kernels - GraniKV (https://arxiv.org/html/2608.15584), CoDec (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.17694). Nothing found that batches schema-composed NON-prefix modules with discontinuous position IDs, so not scooped, but the incremental novelty over existing prefix sharing is thin.

risks: Paper section 3.3 and the code disagree about what is masked: modules are encoded by ONE forward pass over the whole scaffold and then sliced (promptcache/cache_engine.py:221-296), so within a schema each module attends to its predecessors, whereas 3.3 claims attention is 'confined to the span of each prompt module'. Table 1's accuracy preservation may therefore measure a much weaker approximation than advertised. This is both the biggest threat to the paper's claim and the basis of add-on A1; it should be checked empirically in week 1.

The headline 8x configuration is not reachable from a config file: promptcache/cache_engine.py:290-292 always demotes modules to host memory when the target device is a GPU, and TokenSequenceCache.upload()/free() (:65-73) are dead code. Either the GPU-memory bars of Figure 3 came from an unreleased code path or from a trivial edit to line 290 - so 'we reproduced Figure 3' weakens to 'after a one-line change we believe matches the paper'.

The evaluation never exercises cross-request reuse: remove_all_schemas() is called after every entry (eval.py:280, eval_sys.py:363) and schema encoding time is excluded from reported TTFT. The measured speedup is an upper bound assuming an infinitely warm, never-evicted cache; any improvement claim must state amortisation explicitly.

LongBench barely tests modularity: benchmark/longbench.py:105 puts the entire document in a single <module name="context">, so the accuracy evaluation is effectively single-module (prefix) reuse. Multi-module behaviour appears only in the section 5.6 qualitative case studies (examples/*.xml), which carry no metric. New multi-module schemas are needed before any accuracy claim about modular reuse.

Undocumented dataset exclusions: scripts/benchmark_setup.json:25-34 records that lcc, repobench-p and samsum were dropped because 'code syntax interferes with xml syntax of prompt cache' - an inherent fragility of the XML-based PML that the paper never discusses - and lsht/vcsum/dureader for OOM. Expect the same or worse on a 24 GB GPU.

Weak statistical support: eval_sys.py uses 5 entries x 3 repeats per dataset (:305, :318, :29) and eval_acc.py hard-codes limit_entries=3 (:105). get_scores.py:99 computes a std but the paper's tables report none, so Table 1 effect sizes (e.g. 16.63 vs 13.95) may not be separable from noise. Reporting confidence intervals is itself a defensible 'Contemporary paper' fallback.

Gated weights: meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf and codellama/CodeLlama-7b-Instruct-hf (demo.py:27) need HF licence acceptance. The ungated Falcon-7B/MPT-7B fallbacks exist in config/, but MPT needs trust_remote_code=True (promptcache/model/__init__.py:264) and sets use_full_position_ids=True (:275), a materially different and less-exercised code path.

Frozen dependency stack: the repo vendors transformers-4.34 model files (promptcache/model/llama2.py:34 imports ALL_LAYERNORM_LAYERS, :593 keys off config._flash_attn_2_enabled), both removed in later transformers, so the project is locked to a 2023-era stack and needs Python 3.10 rather than the machine's default 3.12. An add-on cannot casually adopt modern transformers, FlashAttention-2 (the FA2 path at llama2.py:413-584 is in fact missing its flash_attn_func import) or SDPA kernels without porting work - relevant to add-on A4 especially.

Hardware mismatch on absolutes: the paper's GPUs (A40 48 GB, A100 40 GB, RTX 4090) all differ from the A5000 in memory and, for the 4090, compute. Only the cache/no-cache RATIO is the claim to reproduce; absolute TTFTs will not match.

Scoop pressure is real and rising: CacheBlend, EPIC, KVLink, A3, CacheClip, CachedAttention, SGLang HiCache and CacheGen collectively cover much of the obvious improvement space around this paper. The defensible angles are the ones grounded in what the ARTIFACT does not do (A1's memory-for-quality trade plus the scaffold-slicing audit; A2's module-granularity tiering), not generic 'make KV reuse better' proposals.

Script rot that will cost a day if not anticipated: eval_sys.py:432-437 has the Figure 3/4 entry points commented out; eval_sys.py:286 and :164 write to directories (benchmark/aaa, benchmark/results_latency) that are never created outside run_latency_eval; eval_sys.py:91-104 hard-codes Llama2-13B cache geometry in run_critical_point regardless of --llm_config_path; get_scores.py:73 reads ./results_13b/ while eval.py:155 writes ./benchmark/results/; Makefile:4 and scripts/benchmark_setup.json:3 point at a nonexistent config/llm_config_llama2.json; and there are no plotting scripts (benchmark/results/README.md is a one-line stub).
